As the custom, although without legal warrant, had grown up. however, I might have felt at liberty to keep the Inscription, had 1 approved of Its be ing on the coinage. But as I did not approve of It, I did not direct that It should again be put on. Of course, the matter of the law Is absolutely In the hands of Qongress and any direction of Congress In the matter, will be Im mediately obeyed. WASHINGTON, Nov. 13.— The com plaint prepared by the North Pacific Lumber association, charging discrim ination and illegal action against prac tically all the Important western and northwestern railroads, wa^ filed with the interstate commerce commission today. It asserts that the Union Pacific and other western and northwestern lines by concert of action absolutely fixes ratos on all forest products from the Pacific northwest to eastern destinations. It alleges that the Great Northern and the Northern Pacific dominate and con trol the Burlington company through ownership of its stock, that the Union Pacific dominates and controls the Ore gon Railroad & Navigation company, the Oregon Short Line and the Southern Pa cific by virtue of ownership of the ma jority of their capital stock and by other devices and arrangements, so that there is no competition between them; that the Southern Pacific dominates and con trols the Oregon & California and the Corvallls & Eastern companies through ownership of the majority of the rail road stock by lease or otherwise. It is asserted that the railroads have advanced rates 5 to 10 cents a hundred pounds, effective on November 1, on all forest products; that the rates are ex cessive, extortionate, prohibitive and dis criminatory, and that if exacted the lum ber Industry of the northwest will be seriously Injured if not destroyed. The complainants aver that they have $60,000,000 capital invested in their indus tries and employ 40,000 people; that their annual payroll aggregates $20,000,000 and that they pay In freight $12,000,000 an nually for 30,000 carloads of forest products. Nov. 18.-In answer to one of the numerous protests which have boon received at the White House against tlie new gold coins which have been coined without the words: "In God we trust," President Roosevelt has written a letter which ho toflay mado public. The letter follows: "When the question of new coinage camo up, we looked Into tho law anil lound there was no warrant therein for putting 'In God we trust' on the coins. As the custom, although without legal warrant, had grown up, however, I might have felt at liberty to keep the inscrlp i"ln had 1 approved of its being on the. coinage. But as I did not approve of It, I did not direct that it should again be put on. "Of course the matter of tho law is ab solutely in the hands of congress and any action in that direction will be immedi ately obeyed. At present there is no war rant in law for the inscription. "My own feeling 111 the matter is due to my very firm conviction that to put such a motto on coins, or to use it in any kin dred manner, not only does no good but does positive harm, and is in effect irrev erent, which comes dangerously close to sacrilege. "A solemn sentence, such as the one in question, should be trcatod and uttered only with that fine reverence which ne.: essarlly implies a certain exaltation of spirit. Any use which tends to cheapen it, and above all, any use which tends to secure its being treated in a spirit of levity is from every standpoint pro foundly to bo regretted. It Is a mottj which is Indeed well to have inscribed on our great national monuments, in our temples of justice, in our executive halls, end in buildings such as thoso at West Point and Annapolis, in short, wherever It will tend to arouse and inspire a lofty emotion in those who looked thereon. "But it seems to mo eminently unwise to cheapen a motto by use on coins such as it would be to cheapen it by use on postage stamps or in advertisements. As regards its irse on the coinage, we have actual experience by which to go. In all my life I have never heard any human speak reverently of this motto on the coins, but I have hundreds of times heard ft used as an occasion ot, and incitement to tho sneering ridicule, which it Is above all things undesirable that so beautiful and exalted a phra&o should excite. "For example, throughout the long con test extending over several decades on the free coinage question, the issuance of this motlo on the coins was a con stant source of jest and ridicule; and this was unavoidable. "Everyone must remember the innu merable cartoons and articles based on phrases like 'In God we trust' for the eight cents; 'In God we trust for the short weight;' 'In God we trust for the thirty-seven centß wo don't pay,' and so forth. "Surely I am well within bounds when I say that a use of the phrase which invited constant levity of this phrase is undesirable. "If congress alters the laws and directs me to replace on the coins the sentence in question, it will be immediately put Into effect, but I trust that the sentiment of the country, the spirit of reverence in the country, will prevent such action be '"fsi^ned)' "THEODORE ROOSEVELT." New York, Nov. 23.—A mystery that may. never be fully solved. surrounds the death of Nicholas Smith, a wealthy New York manufacturer and his wife, who were found shot to death In their home at New Castle early today. The bodies were found by firemen who had been summoned to fight a blaze In the cellar of the residence, which had been started by the murder ers In the belief that the bodies of the victims would be Incinerated and all traces of crime thus swept away. That only two persons were directly concerned in the tragedy Is the belief of the police but whether It was the husband or the wife who fired the fatal shots and applied the torch, they do not know. Theory points to the wife as the slayer, but there are circumstances which would make it appear that she could not have been the guilty one. In view of all these perplexing Indi cations. the officials who thus far have Investigated the case, decline to ad vance any opinion. They say that If a solution ever Is reached, It must be reached by the coroner. Two servants In the house say that the Smith's had a quarrel last evening. Several hours later, long after midnight, shots were heard. The servants told the police to day that they made no attempt to in vestigate the cause of the shooting or Its results as they feared to leave their rooms. They were found there when the firemen came and could throw little light on the tragedy. Mrs. Smith's body was found In her bed. She was lying as If asleep with both hands folded beneath her head. There was a bullet wound In the breast. Just across the threshold. In an adjoining room, lay the body of the husband. He was partly dressed. After the first hasty examination, the police concluded that Smith had killed his wife, fired the house and then ended his own life. l*ater, however, a note found in Mrs. Smith's bedroom put an entirely dif ferent aspect on the affair. Lovingly, Grace." An Inventory of all the valuables In the same handwriting as in the note, also war. found. That a determined attempt to de stroy by fire had been made, was evi dent from an examination of the part ly burned cellar. Marlon, Nov., 23—(Special)—The local banks began Wednesday to fur nish currency to pay for cotton and the market has assumed its normal condition. VAST SUM IS DEMANDED PHILADELPHIA MINT CALLED ON FOR $60,000,000 MUST TURN OUT 4000 COINB AN HOUR Record Breaking Amount of Bullion Will Be In Vaults After Coinage of Required Double Eagles Special Correspondence to The Herald. PHILADELPHIA, Nov. 18. George B. Cortelyou, secretary of the United States treasury, has demanded not less than $60,000,000 In gold double eagles to be delivered within the next three months, and the Philadelphia mint stands ready with Its great facilities to arise to the occasion. Day and night coiners, assayers, weigh ers and the countless other specialised workers who make up the staff of the mint have been working overtime— some of them fourteen horns a day— since the order came. In less than two weeks, de spite the fact that there have been per emptory demands for the almost unlim ited coinage of dimes, quarters, half dol lars and silver dollars, two millions In gold double eagles have already been de livered. When the order came requiring delivery by Tuesday, November 12, of $2,000,000 In double eagles, all employed In the mintIng of money were ordered to "get busy." Massive new machinery was brought into play with fine success, and the necessary amount of gold coined had been carefully packed away In glittering piles three days later. Then everybody was put to work upon more double eagles. The efficiency of the new machinery In opening and shutting the split collar, a rtevirfl for putting stars on the edge of the newly designed double eagles, was well attested In the emergency. There are forty-six stars on the edge of each piece, because of the approaching advent of the new state of Oklahoma to the Union. The machinery of the mint Is capable of grinding out 4000 of these pieces In an hour. As soon as $150,000 in half dollars and a similar amount in quarters are sent out from the mint, and this will be within a few days, the attention of the entire working force will be devoted to the task of meeting the requirement for gold. When the two millions in gold double eagles had been coined there were still $24,000,000 in available bullion In the vaults of the mint. On Wednesday, while a part of this was being rapidly converted into double eagles, Cashier Joseph D. Murphy of the Philadelphia mint received word to look out for the arrival at the Institu tion of $10,000,000 more In gold. Do Not Fear Robbers Instantly word was passed around, and when, an hour later, a wagon of tho United States Express company quietly halted at a side gate there was a force of mint employes ready to help the men in jumpers and overalls to land their precious burden safely in the massive vaults. The gold was part of the glittering cargo brought over by the Lusltanla, and it had arrived at the Reading terminal In express cars shortly after noon. It was then conveyed In ordinary express wagons to the mint. Cashier Murphy smiled indulgently when asked what pre cautions were taken to prevent the loot of one of the treasure wagonß. "In a crowded city like Philadelphia," ne said, "It would be impossible for a theft to occur on one df the express wagons. The Idea of a 'holdup' is out of the question, as deliveries to the mint are never made except In broad daylight. Now, It follows, If there is any loss it must be the work of a sneak thief and one who would be an extraordinarily rapid worker. The wagons are In charge of two men, and even If a thief managed for a moment to elude their vig.'lance his shrift would be short. It is no easy task to net away with bullion as it is packed. "Try for yourself," continued Mr. Murphy, pointing to a heap of mysterious looking boxes. "That one contains a bar of virgin gold. Hold it in your arms for five minutes." Half that time sufficed to prove the cashier's contention. "It would not be pleasant to run down the street with a howling mob at your heels and still hold on to the booty, would it?" "The story of tho armed express guards," he went on, "is on a par with the story that every visitor to the mint Is searched before leaving. In the same connection I may mention another amus ing example of florid imagination run riot. When the mint was on Chestnut street, near Broad, pedestrians frequently stopped to look at dense yellow fumes that sometimes ascended from the chim ney. They were simply one of the results of certain refining processes to which we subjected all gold that was under a standard of purity. But there was a wonderful story circulated to the effect that those fumes carried minute gold grains and that in consequence the gov ernment had a claim upon sweepings from the roofs of various commercial es tablishments in the Immediate vicinity." NEW YORK, Nov. 28.— That the esti mate that 50,000 emigrants will leave New York this week for European ports Is far below the number that will probably sail is the opinion expressed by Gustkv H. Schwab of tho North German-Lloyd Steamship company. At least 60,000 and perhaps 70,000 will sail, according to Mr. Schwab's figures. The Pennsylvania railroad alone brought more than 2000 to New York today. "Immigration regulates itself and needs no stimulus from the steamship com panies." said Mr. Schwab. 'When times arc good in thin country und there is plenty of employment they come over; when there is a lack of work the laborers return to their own country." Every steamer sailing yesterday was filled to its capacity with steerage pas sengers, and although the steerage rate was again raised, this time from 131 to J36. it made no difference with the num ber of people demanding tickets. Carry ing passengers, even in the steerage, is more remunerative than carrying freight, and a number of the small lines are fit ting up the holds of their ships for the accommodation of passengers and are leaving freight behind. Several steamers that have heretofore carried only freight are now carrying steerage passengers. This was the case with the Cambrian of the Red Btar line, which sailed yester day with 1000 steerage passengers. ' A curious feature of the situation 1b that the number of immigrants arriving in New York this month is greater than for any November on record. It Is be lieved most of these made their plans before the great exodus began and that as soon as the vanguard of the present horde reaches Europe there will be a great falling off In the traffic in this di rection. Washington, Dec., 11—The annual message of President Roosevelt was read today In both Houses of Con gress and practically no business was attempted by either body beyond lis tening to the message. The galleries of both the Senate and House were crowded at the beginning of the ses sion of each body. In the main, the attendance was well maintained until the last sentences of the document had fallen from the lips of the official readers. Senators and members were supplied with printed copies of the message and many of them followed the clerks reading with scrupulous care. The reading con sumed about two and one quarters hours In each branch. The Houses did not today follow up the lead of yesterday In the Matter of Introduction of many bills, but several were presented. In the Senate so far, no bills have been Introduced, but It Is probably that the flood will break out In that body tomorrow. Speaker Cannon treated the House to a surprise In announcing the mem bership of the committee on banking and currency. This advance formation of that committee led to the conclusion on the part of many that It was his Intention to press financial legislation, but those who are close to the Speaker say that his only purpose was to af ford a depository for petitions and let ters bearing upon the currency ques tion. Appalling Loss of Life— Little Hope That Any of the Entombed Laborers Has Escaped Awful Fate By Associated Press. MONONGAH, W. Va., Dec. 6. — That no fewer than 400 miners were killed by an explosion of black damp in mines Nos. 6 and 8 of the Consolidated Coal company of Baltimore at this place is now conceded by those who take the most hopeful and con servative view of the disaster. Of the victims six dead bodies had been taken from mine No. 6 at midnight and six others were piled up in the entry awaiting the completion of facilities for bringing them to the surface. From mine No. 8 at the same hour, fourteen bodies had been removed, and a number of others are ready to be brought out as soon as ar rangements can be completed. Three cha— ed bodies lying In the Im prbvised morgue, four badly injured men and 493 r.-.on imprisoned by tons of coal, rock and mine debris In the depths of the hills surrounding this mining town, with the chances all against a single one of them being alive, is the most accurate summary obtainable tonight of the results of a mine explosion today, which, in all probability, was attended by greater loss of life than any former dis aster in the history of the bituminous coal mining Industry of America. All Men at Work The explosion occurred shortly after 10 o'clock today, after the full force of 500 men had gone to work In the two mines affected. These two mines are No. 6 and No. 8 of the Consolidated Coal company, located on opposite sides of the west fork 01 the river, at this place, but merged in their underground workings by a headi.'ij.and on the surface by a great steel tipple and a bridge. The finding of the three bodies and the four dying men is the only reward of the strenuous and uninterrupted work on the part of the large rescuing forces that immediately set to work at every possible point. The three living men, while unable to give any detailed report of the disaster, state that Immediately back of them when they began their frantic struggle for liberty there was a large number of men engaged In a similar struggle, while still further back In the workings there was a larger number 'of whom they know nothing. Others Farther Underground It is the opinion of the mine officials and others familiar with mining that these seven men had not penetrated the mine as far as had the majority of the day shift when the explosion occurred, and that they headed for and reached tho main entrance before the heavy cavein that now blocks the entrance not more than a few hundred feet of the maic opening of mine No. 6. As to the miners referred to by tho tcscucd men as having been alive when last seen it is believed they were caught back of a heavy cavein and could noi have survived more thnn a few minutes in the deadly gases with which the entry filled as soon as the ventilating system was interrupted. There is more hope for those in mbre remote sections of tha mine, as they may have reached work ings where fresh air is supplied by other openings, but at best, only the slender hope is entertained for the survival of any one of the men in the mine when the debris can be cleared awaf and communi cation with the outside re-established. One Thousand Employed The two mines regularly employ 1000 men, working in two shifts, 800 during tha day and 500 during the night, and the best information obtainable at this time is that the entire day force had gone to work this morning and that all were caught. * It was shortly after 10 o'clock when the explosion occurred, , and at that hour even the latest of the straggling force is cus tomarily at work, according to mine of ficials. Beyond these figures the company offi cials do not attempt to give estimates. The general opinion in thu town Is that the number of dead and imprisoned will reach 500. A few persons believe this number will be exceeded, claiming that more than half of the total force worked during the day, while, on the other hand, some think the number will be smaller. How It Happened There is much speculation as to the cause of the explosion, but the generally accepted theory is that it resulted from black damp, scientifically known as methane. It is believed that a miner at tempted to set off a blast, which blew out and Ignited an accumulation of the dead ly gas, and that this, in turn, ignited the coal dust, a highly inflammable substance found In greater or less quantities in all West Virginia mines. However, all explanations of the cause up to this time are necessarily specula •' tive. Only a thorough investigation after the mine Is reopened will disclose the cause, If It Is ever ascertained. The explosion affected both mines, and so far as now known appears to have done about as much damage in one as In the other. It has rot been established in which it originated. Evidencing the terrific force of the con cussion, props in the entry of No. 6 mine, supporting the roof, were not only shat tered and torn from their position, but were blown out of the entry and to the east side of the river. Other evidence of the awful force is shown In every sec tion of the mines visited by the rescuerE. Huge quantities of rock and coal have been loosened and hurled in every open ing. It is rumored here that mine officials have ordered 380 coffins shipped to Mo nongah as toon as possible. Worst in History This accident Is said to be the first wherein a loss of life occurred by ex plosion in the history of the region com prising some sixty mines, owned and operated by the Consolidated Coal com pany. In an explosion at the Berryburg mine, forty miles south, a tributary com pany two years ago nineteen men lost their lives. No. 8 mine was opened two years ago and was considered the most modern mine in central West Virginia. It was entirely equipped with electricity and considered absolutely safe. Electric motors were used, while the mine throughout was electric lighted and elec tric mining apparatus was used entirely. Mining experts, a large corps of doctors and others familiar with mining mattera hold out practically no hope to waiting friends that a single person In the shafts of. the mine at the time of the explosion has escaped death. Special Trains Ready Special trains are ready to bring the wounded to the hospitals hero as fast as possible. A hospital was arranged ut the opening of the mine, where the wounded will receive attention. Several men were practically blown out of mlno No. t> through an airhole. Their escape was miraculous. Twenty doctors from Fair mont are now on the ground and every attention is being given the men. The town of Monongah has a population of about 6000, and while for the most part the miners are of foreign birth there are still many American workmen. Tha coal company is one of the largest com panies of the kind in the country and Is capitalized at about $20,000,000. They have upward of 100 producing properties. S. P. Tha distance saved is about four miles, but a, far greater saving is accomplished through the absence of curves and cross ings of heavily traveled streets. MONONGAH, W. Va., Dec. B,— But fifty three bodies had been recovered from mines No. 6 and No. 8 of tho Fairmont Coal company when darkness closed over the little town of Monongah tonight. On account of fire in mine No. 8, and immi nent danger of an explosion In mine No. 6, all rescue work has been suspended for the night. Fifty-six hours had elapsed since the awful explosion, and a majority" of the bodies brought to the surface were in a terrible condition, necessitating almost Immediate burial. It is now believed the number of dead will not bo over 400. A thorough investigation was made by the company today, and It was discovered that many miners believed to have been entombed escaped because they had not gone to work Friday, after Thursday's holiday. A score or more of these men have re ported to the officials during tho past twenty-four hours. S Shortly after 5 o'clock this afternoon fire broke out again in mine No. 8, and the rescuers were at once ordered to the surface. Thousands of sightseers from the sur rounding towns had gathered about the openings. Through megaphones tho crowds we^c notified of the fire and the danger of another explosion, but they re« fused to leave, and It was with great dif ficulty that the special police, assisted by miners, forced these people to seek plaTces of safety. Efforts were then di rected toward extinguishing the fire, and it was thought that it will be subdued within a few hours. One Hundred Bodies Located It was said by members of the rescuing parties that over a hundred bodies have been lpcated in both mines and that they will be brought to the surface as soon as the fire has been extinguished. ACTIVITIES OF WEEK ARE REASSURING REPORTS SHOW LARGE RESERVES TOTAL GOLD IS 60 PER CENT OF CIRCULATION Limiting Issues of Securities and Improvement in New York Bank Statement Aid Restoration of Confidence By Associated Press. NEW YORK, Dec. B.— The events of tho past week In tho financial world have, been such as usually mark the gradual return of confidence and the restoration of normal ccndltions in the banks. The decision of the secretary of the treasury to issue only about $40,000,000 of the $100, 00,000 in new securities which he ex pressed a willingness to Issue If condi tions required; the disclosure of unusu ally strong reserves by country banks re porting to the comptroller of the cur rency, the decline in the currency premi um, and the improvement in the New York bank statement, have all been fea tures of the week which have tended toward stability and reassurance. The action of the secretary of the treas ury in limiting the issues of securities was a part of the original plan recom mended to him to meet the situation by a n>Holute and adequate measure, but to carry the execution of the measure no further than circumstances required. The result of the limiting of the issue of the Panama 2 per cent bonds to $25,000,000 and the one-year treasury certificates to about $15,000,000 will be to considerably simplify the problem of the treasury management, and money market conditions during the spring. , Plethora Expected It is anticipated by far-sighted bankers Here that there will be a plethora of money soon instead of a dearth, and that it will be necessary to reduce In some way the large volume of currency which has been brought Into use during the crisis. The increase in money in circulation outside the treasury, as shown by the monthly statement of the treasury de partment for November, was $131,872,887. Of this amount the increase in gold in the country is computed at about $72,000, 00, including domestic production as well as importations from abroad. The other principal form of Increase Is In bank cir culation, In which an increase of $7,633, 521 was obtained by the disbursement of bank notes held In the treasury cash, and $4G,287,730 was obtained by actual increase In the notes issued by the comptroller and outstanding. There have been fears In some quarters that if anything approximating $100,000,000 in new bank -notes were issued upon the securities of the new one-year certifi cates, the resulting inflation would expel gold in largo amounts after the credits established by the crop movement were exhausted. This danger will be reduced to a mini mum by the relatively small issues made by the treasury, an&At small amounts in gold should be exported it is felt that they could be spared. In view of the large gold resources In the country to which President Roosevelt calleu attention In announcing the new loans. Look for Increase The total gold in the country reported by the last treasury statement is $1,661, 714,(19, which Is equal to more than 60 per cent of the total money in circula tion. Some further Increase In bank cir culation is expected here upon the Pana ma bonds and the treasury certificates, but it Is believed the bonds will be de posited In many cases as security for the public money .which has been left with the banks, and will not be employed as a basis for circulation until the one-year certificates are cancelled in the spring, when money to be withdrawn from th<» banks by the treasury for the redemption of the certificates will release the bonds, and the latter can then be substituted for the certificates as security for circu lation. If this proves to be the case, the increase in bank circulation will not be very great during the next few months, and may even turn downward as soon as it becomes apparent that the banks have a large accumulation of cash for which there Is little demand. The curtailment of the Issues by the government will reduce the cost of the one-year certificates to about $300,000. This estimate Is based upon tho cancel lation of $10,000,000 of the certificates In six months, which will make the Inter est paid only V/i per cent, while the full interest of 3 per cent Is paid on the re maining $5,000,000. Reserves Are Large The reports of the condition of the na tional banks on December 3, which are being published in various localities, and are gradually reaching the comptroller of the currency, are verifying the antici pation of the leading bankers that large reserves would be disclosed in the in terior banks, that the disclosures would tend to restore confidence and that the banks would be willing to release such excess reserves after making their state ments. A rough calculation of the re ports of the Chicago banks, including some state banks. Indicates reserves of nearly 35 per cent. About the same pro portion is reported from New Orleans, and still higher reserves at smaller places, where the law requires 15 per cent. The fact that two failures of national banks of a certain degree of importance have occurred during the week without apparently causing any shock to confi dence, even in their own localities, and still less In the financial centers, Is re garded here as another favorable indica tion of the financial markets. The increase of $4,671,000 in actual cash in th 4 New York clearing house banks Is regarded here as one of the symptoms that the currency crisis, as such, Is prac tlcaily over. The reduction of loans by about $11,600,000, is also considered a favorable Indication of diminishing presThe increase In the required reserve by $6,779,000 reduces the deficit in New York reserves to $46,210,000, and part of this will be covered by gold yet to arrive. Legislation Not Looked For Not much is expected among New York bankers In the way of currency legisla tion by congress at the present session. The fact that the presidential election Is approaching and that there is wide diver sity of view as to the proper form of new legislation, leads to the belief that the subject will be only considered without final action during this session. The necessity of some Important meas ure of reform is quite generally recog nized, but the growth of sentiment for a strong central bank is checking in some degree the movement for giving wider powers of note issue to the existing na tional banks. Some bankers declare that the two measures are not incompatible, and that if a moderate power of issue in emergency were given to existing banks by the present congress this need not in terfere with the creation of a strong cen tral bank as soon a« the subject has been thoroughly considered by the people. The committee appointed, by Governor Hughes to Improve tne legislation of the state of New York In regard to trust companies has nearly completed its la bors, and. will recommend some Important changes. A very considerable Increase In trust company reserves will undoubtedly be recommended. It is also desired to bring the trust companies Into some form of co-operation with the clearing house, though it may not be possible to provide by legislation that this shall be compul sory. ROMANTIC COURTSHIP NEARSEND LOS ANGELES GIRL AWAITS SOLDIER LOVER PIECE OF HARDTACK MAY UNITE TWO HEARTS Pretty Young Woman Places Name on Cracker, Which Is Found by Engineer In the Far East The Journey of a piece of hardtack front Los Angeles to the Philippines is the cause of the faster beating of one sol dier's heart with each passing day that brings nearer the time when he can again tread the soil of California, aftar an absence of two years among savages, whose welfare has been intrusted to the care of Uncle Sam with the acquirement of vast and strange possessions in the tar east. And it all came about from the prank of a pretty girl. The soldier has never seen the girl, and neither has she seen him. The medium through which the long-dis tance acquaintance that has developed into a more tender affection was made was a cracker, a common piece of hard tack, the substantiality of which delights the penurious soul of the commissary de partment and makes the soldier deplore his position and his jaws crack in pro test. The soldier is Howard Taylor, a member of company C, engineer corps, stationed on the Island of Mindanao, Philippines. Uooa fortune deait the utuub, aim early one August morning Taylor, as he placed the piece of hardtack to his lips, saw written upon it the name of a girl and underneath the name and address. Many Letters Exchanged What more natural than that he, pining for the refining Influences of home life, living in a country where danger is ever present, should write to the young woman? And, again, what more natural than that she, acting from the motives of pure sym pathy in a woman's heart, should,, reply? That the initial letters should be followed by others and that they should become more affectionate is, of course, to be sup posed. Early In August Miss Ruth Walker, a pretty 18-year-old girl living at 646 Kohler street, while in one of the large cracker factories of Los Angeles, wrote her name and address on the piece of hardtack. The cracker, packed with thousands of others, was shipped to the supply depart ment of Mare island and thence made the long journey across the Pacific. At Manila it was placed on a narrow gauge train and sent into the interior and then transshipped to an army wagon. After miles of travel over the government's new roads it reached, together with tons of other supplies, the little vil lage of Pautar, Mindanao, and fell Into the hands of the commissary sergeant of company C, engineer corps. Fate placed It In Howard Taylor's rations and fa'e stopped him in the act of destroying It in the usual way. Tells of Conditions Taylor took the first opportunity to write, and the letter, traveling by steamer to the Island of Moro, then to Manila, began Its long trip across the Pacific and reached the Walker home in mid-Septem ber. Since then letters have been com paratively frequent, for mall travels faster than supplies. Taylor's letters are Interesting, telling of conditions In the far interior of th.j islands and of the life of the soldiers in camp. Pautar, he says, is situated in one of the wildest spots on Mindanao Island. His company has been stationed at that place for almost two years, and every member of It Is constantly on the alert, for savages surround them and take ad vantage of every opening to dash In an! cut to pieces every man within reach. He expresses little hope for the future civilization of the Moros who inhabit tho islands, and, although he does not bellevo in their extermination by the sword, ha thinks the tribal warfare constantly goinK en and the manner in which they live will have the effect of diminishing them until they will be regarded as one of the lost tribes. Clothing at a Premium Each district, he says, has a datto, or chief, with anywhere from fifty to 50,000 slaves. They also have from three to 100 wives. ~ Clothing, it seems,' is at a premium, the people wearing anywhere from nothing to almost nothing. As a source of amusement the men of company C have tamed two monstrous snakes, one of which is twenty-five feet In length, the other eighteen feet. They also have a cage filled with monkeys. These monkeys have been taught, after much labor, to act as guards, and al though they are not on Uncle Sam's pay roll their services are not without re ward, for they are fed and petted beyond measure. The outer guard lines are placed at a great distance from the main body of troops, a mile sometimes separating tho camp from the little squads upon whose vigilance depends the lives of thousands. The guards carry monkeys to their tem porary stations, and there the little ani mals are released. Make Good Guards The Moro is one of their worst enemies, and they never stray far from their sol dier friends. Whether it is from an In born desire to create a racket or because* of an appreciation of danger, the mon keys nevertheless, at tho first sign of danger, set up such a chattering that the whole squad Is aroused, while the ani mals scamper back to camp, carrying a noisy message of threatening danger. Burdette Preaches In. teresting Sermon at Temple Bap tist Church — Shows How the Work Serves Mammon Robert J. Burdette preached on the topic "Religious Veneer" at the Temple Baptist church yesterday. He took for his text Matthew, 22:20: "Jesus saith unto them. Whose is this image and super scription? They say unto him, Cae sar's." Dr. Burdette said in part: "And that was all of the coin that be longed to Caeßar— something on the out side of it. Something a man at Caesar's command put on it. "Long centuries before Caesar was, the voice of the Lord God proclaimed: 'The silver is mine and the gold is mine.' Let Caesar or Judas, Dives or Lazarus scratch what little vainglorious Inscrip tion he will upon its surface. "If all the religion we have can be minted on the outside of a silver dollar, it won't do us a bit of good to put it on, and it won't do us a particle of harm to file It off. "One of the president's critics— she is the richest woman In America— said the other day, commenting upon the removal of the phrase, 'In God we trust' from the new gold coins: Makes Men Think " 'The president often speaks without thinking.' "Coming from the sex which is noted for always subjecting impulse to calm, deliberate, careful. Judicial analysis, and then speaking with conservative restraint and non-committal caution, her state ment Is entitled to respectful considera tion. "But whether the president speaks without thinking or not, he seldom speaks without making all the rest of the 1 men in the country think, or think they think, which is as far as some men ever get on their way to intellectual pro cesses, and it is also to be noted they speak Just ns promptly, Just aa impul sively, Just as hair trlggery as the presi dent can be accused of doing. "The first time I saw the phrase, as I remember, was on the old trade ¦ dollar, which was worth only 92 cents. That started the irreverent Jokes and profane cartoons to which the president refers in his letter explaining why he ordered the omission of the phrase from the new issue of coin. No Reverence in Words "There is no more reverence in the words on our money than there is in texts of Scripture printed on cards and scattered about the street like pearls to be trampled under the feet of— er— men. "All our coins of higher value bear the inscription now. And there has never been a time in the history of America when we trusted God less and served mammon more than we have done in the past few years. "When we remember what our utter ignoring of the noble sentiment and our base, insane, sordid worship of the coin which bears it has done for us; how It has lowered our standard of commercial Integrity; debased our business life; cor rupted our sense of honor; polluted our politics; sent representatives In congress and United States senators, members of state legislatures and mayors of great cities to the penitentiaries; how it has made thle proud and mighty nation a hissing and a byword among the peoples of the earth: how It has covered us with shame as with a garment— we ought to be glad to see the hypocritical whine erased from our coin. It has no place there. Let Lives Speak "You might as well inscribe 'Blessed are the pure in heart" over the doorway of a brothel Just because it is a beautiful text. When tears of penitence have washed the stains from our money; when the 'Napoleons of finance," in the spirit of Zaccheus, have restored fourfold all they have stolen from widow and or phan and laborer; when we have made our double eagles weigh as much as the tiny copper coin Jesus saw fall from the thin fingers of the poor widow into the great treasury of the splendid temple; when the souls of the money changers, scourged from the very shadow of the house of God by the indignation of the Son have been washed with the balm of healing grace, we may consistently re place the declaration of trust. ST. PETERSBURG, Dec. 10.-Before a brilliant assemblage of old comrades In arms Lieut. Gen. Stoessel was today placed on trial to answer with his life and reputation for the loss of Port Arthur January 1, 1905. In firm tones and with quiet manner the general pleaded not guilty to the charge of needlessly sur rendering the fortress and thereby hu miliating the Russian army. The court was convoked by Judge Doubakoff. He declared it to be the duty of the court to proceed with the trial ot the four officers charged with the respon sibility of surrendering the fortress on terms dishonorable to the garrison and humilitating to the prestige of Russia. He then called {he roll of 200 witnesses. Including Gen. Kuropatkin and Vice Ad mlral Wlren. Several of the witnesses were absent, hut the court decided to proceed with the trial. The entire afternoon was taken up with the reading of the voluminous in dictment. The trial took plnce in the auditorium of the Army and Navy club. The room resembled more a soclul gathering of of ficers of high rank than the scene of a court-martial. Among those present were sailors and witnesses, Gen. Kuropatkin, Gen. Rennenkampf, Vice Admiral Wiren and scores of other prominent leaders In the Russo-Japanese war. Witnesses Wear Medals There were also present 200 officers and soldiers who had been at Port Arthur and who . today were clad in their ¦ full dress uniforms with stars and decorations. Gen. Stoessel was alone in civil attire, and this made him conspicuous. : ; He wore proudly around 'his neck the \ cordon of the i mili tary order of St. George which was con ferred upon him rby the emperor : during the siege, ; andironhis breast • waspinned the cross of George 111, awarded for con spicuous bravery in .frontier work. , ¦ The same coveted | decorations . was . worn by many of the witnesses and spectators. ¦ : ¦ Empty sleeves and crutches, especially among the men who had been at Port Arthur, showed that many of them had seen hard service during the war. The other accused officers, Gens. Riss and Smirnoff, came to the court clad in their uniforms. Gen. Smirnoff, jrho is a bitte. enemy of Gen. Stoessel, ostentatlonsly seated himself as far away as possible from the central figure of the proceed ings. One or two incidents showed the attitude of the court to bfe unfavorable to Stoessel His personal request that two additional witnesses be called in was dismissed with out ceremony. Stoessel had 8000 able-bodied men to defend the fortifications, and the cold winds at the time made it difficult for the soldiers even to hold their rifles. Gen. Nalen, the other witness excluded, is the author of a deposition similar to that of Dr. Roseanoff. The general commanded the firing line at Port Arthur. Witnesses of all ranks declared the trial to be an insult to Gen. Stoessel and to his army. A prominent colonel said: "If Stoessel is guilty we are all guilty." MeetIngs of the executive committee of the> Goldlleld miners' union and of the Gold fleld mine owners' association were held tonight. It is believed here that President Roose velt is responsible for the decision of Gen. Funston to come to Goldfleld, thac the Intention is to take the conduct of affairs out of the hands of Governor Sparks and the Esmeralda county offi cials, and that martial law will be de clared in Goldfleld immediately upon the arrival of Gen. Funston. The mine own ers are fearful of the consequence when the attempt to open the mines is made, t«t they are apparently determined to carry out their intentions to resume op erations Thursday. The arrival of Gov. Sparks In Goldfleld early this afternoon has led to many rumors of impending trouble, but beyond the little excitement caused by tha presence of the governor two days ahead of the time announced, nothing has transpired today to materially affect the situation. Funston to Be Commander Indications are that the military au thorities are preparing to proclaim mar tial law. The situation then will be taken out of the hands of Gov. Sparks, who is not in touch with the sheriffs office, an 4 Gen. Funston, who is to ar rive here from San Francisco Thursday, to personally take charge of the troops and handle the situation, will be in ab solute control. Thla afternoon Gov. Sparks, accompanied by his representa tive here. Col. William Cox. went In an automobile to the headquarters of Col. Reynolds, and an hour was spent in going over the situation in Goldfleld. Col. Rey nolds said that he has not yet obtained a thorough grasp of the situation, or learned all of the conditions which led to the sending of troops. Gov. Sparks was visited at the hotel where he is staying by many of the prominent mine owners and members and officials of the Goldfleld Mine Owners' association, but he denied that any official conference between himself and officials of the association has taken place. Ha was also visited by officers of the miners' union, who assured him that the union will do all in its power to prevent violence, and has been, and still is, earnestly endeavoring to effect a peace able settlement of the difficulties be tween themselves and the operators of the mines. Preparing for Work The universal impression is that martial law will not be declared until after the arrival of Gen. Funston, but that pre parations will be made at once for the work which will have to be performed by the troops as soon as such action Is taken. Doubtless a search of the camp will be made for weapons and ammuni tion alleged to be hidden by some of the desperate element among the miners, and the districts where the miners live will be patrolled by the soldiers night and day. The Mine Owners' association offi cials still assert that the original in tention to reopen the mines on Thurs day morning will be carried out, and that enough men have already been se cured to carry on the attempt, although it is admitted that the number of men who have already signed the new agreement as individuals is small and that their hope lies in the supposition that after a few have gone back many others will soon follow. It is definitely known that at least 500 men have been secured in the min ing camps of California, principally In Calaveras county, through the agency of the Thief detective bureau, and are being held in readiness to come to Goldfleld on two days' notice. Preparations For Departure of Big Fleet Have Been Completed And Monday Will Witness The Actual Start. Old Point Comfort. Va., Dec., 12— Final word of "Ready" was flashed from every vessel In the battleship fleet today. In Its last analysis, this signal meant that sixteen most power ful armor-dads of the American navy were ready to start next Monday morn ing on their projected cruise to the western seas It meant that hulls are sweet and clean, that giant compound engines are restless to be at their task; that officers and men are trained to the hour; that bunkers are overflowing with coal, that larders are choked with ship's provisions and that magaxlne doors are closed upon the greatest stores of ammunition ever placed on board American vessels of war. If the ships were destined for Im mediate conflict, little more could be done to make them ready for the fray. Now that all Is ready, officers and men alike are anxious to get away. There Is an entire absence of enthusi asm, but a manifest atmosphere of serious devotion to duty surrounding the departure of the fleet. The orders and the published itinerary offers lit tle prospect of entertainment or amusement en route. When the fleet was first ordered to prepare for the Pacific voyage, the navigators of each ship were supplied with especially pre pared charts leading down the South Atlantic coast through the treacherous waters of Magellan and along the Pacific coast to Han Frahclsco. Several weeks ago these charts were supple mented by others showing the way to Manila. Then more recently have come lately revised charts capable of guiding the fleet all the way to Gibraltar. The furnishing of these charts has given rise to gossip that the fleet Is destined eventually to cir cle the globe. The ordnance officers have prob ably accomplished the most difficult duties In preparing for the cruise. They have had to see to the storage of more than 2,000.000 pounds of am munition In the carefully protected magazines and to the Installation of the new and secret fire control system. Armor piercing projectiles filled with explosive D. said to be the most power ful and effective of all the secret formulas in the possession of the navy's experts have been placed aboard the ships and the vast supplies of smokeless powder charges have been stowed away under the double Pro tection Of silken bags and copper Mned cyclindrical tanks. , One of the greatest problems which confronted the ordnance experts had to do with the storage of the Heavy charges of gun cotton taken along to load the score of harbor mines which each battleship carries. GOLDFIELD, Ney., Dec. 12.— The first day of the attempt to reopen the mines of Goldfield without the aid 'of the West ern Federation of Miners has passed and there has been not a single Instance of attempted violence or disorder in the camp. Unarmed pickets of the Goldfleld miners' union have approached as close to the scene of operations as the armed guards of the Mine Owners' association would permit, and have succeeded in in ducing some of those who had signed the agreement to return to work to violate that agreement and leave the mines. Gen. Frederick Funston arrived at noon and his coming seems to have helped the situation greatly and to have strengthened the constantly grow ing impression that the fearful incidents of. strikes In other mining camps are not to be repeated here. It is stated tonight that the leaders of the strike have secured what evidence they want to prosecute some of the mining operators under a state statute, which makes it a crime, punishable by a fine of not less than twenty, nor more than one hundred and fifty days, or both, to require any employe to promise or agree not to become a member or remain a member of any labor organi zation. Arrests may be expected at any time, it is said by some, while others characterize the whole report of probable arrests as a bluff. Funston in Conference After a conference with President Charles H. Mackinnon, of the Goldfleld Miners' union. Gen. Funston sent a report to Washington tonight regarding the situation In Goldfield. The conference with President Mackinnon took place at 8 o'clock and was the last of a series of conferences which Gen. Funston has been holding since his arrival here today at 12:30. Governor Sparks, Col. Reynolds, in command of the troops, Acting President Dowlen and Secretary Em, of the Gold fleld Mine Owners' association, and others were called into these conferences and Gen. Funston wasted no time In acquainting himself with an outline, at least, of the conditions that prevail here. While Gen. Funston refused to say to a representative of the Associated Press what is contained In his report to Wash ington, he said that it contains nothing In regard to the probable length of the stay of the troops in Goldfleld, but would be confined to the needs for them at the present time. "The regulars will be hero at least until after the arrival of the labor com missioners from AVashington," said Gen. Funston. "This means that they will be here for another week, and I have no doubt they will remain m.uch longer than that, or at least a portion of the number now here will. Hearing All Sides "I am hearing all sides of the question as to the necessity for the troops In Goldfield at this time to preserve peace and order, and it is too soon after my arrival for me to have obtained an opinion. My report tonight will simply set forth my view of the situation as I have obtained it from the people whom I have seen today. "It must be understood that I am not here to go into the merits of the dispute between the mine owners and the miners. That is what the commissioners are com ing from Washington for. They doubtless will go deeply Into the merits of the grievances of both sides. but I am simply going to determine whether the continued presence of the troops, or at least a part of them, In Goldfleld, will prevent disorder and riot and bloodshed. 1 am convinced that the presence of the troops thus far has been a necessary pre caution. "Martial law should be a last resort, and I will not advocate it until there hns been great violence committed and the local authorities have proven themselves unable to stop any outrages, such as the destruction of life or property. Either the president or the governor of the state must declare martial law, and in the event that it be the governor ,1 gball consider that the regulars are at liis service, jnst as would be the state militia, provided Nevada had such an Institution. In fact, it is my idea that the regulars are here to take the place of a state militia during the present crisis. Reynolds in Command "Col. Reynolds remains iri command of the troops now encamped here, and 1 am here to make a report on the situa tion and to direct things in the event of serious trouble. "No man can say what amount of trouble is to grow out of this situation, of course, but I am trying to get at the possibilities fur the trouble, and for that reason I sought an Interview with President Mackinnon and other leaders In the local miners' union in order to hear their side of It, and to judge for myself of their frame of mind and dis position to bring about any dis turbances." FRESNO, Dec. 14.— What was prob ably the beginning of the war of the shippers of California on the Soutn ern Pacific railroad for the betterment of transportation conditions and the stampin-r out of allsged rebates ana discriminations burst forth this after noon in Einstein hall at the convention of the counties committee of the Cali fornia promotion commission. The first shot wna fired by Isidoi Jacobs of San Francisco, president or the Good Government league, who, during the lively skirmish which fol lowed, promised that startling exposi tions of tlie railroad's methods would be given to the people of the state within the next few weeks. After the read^g of several papers on the "Marketing of California Pro ducts" Jacobs arose and read an amend ment to the resolution of the regular committee, in which was demanded "the stopping of special privileges and illegal amendments to the laws of the. state in regard to common carriers, ' and a demand that the state officials follow the policy of President Roose velt and the work of the interstate commission in regulating railroads. Fight Over Resolution That short amendment was offered because the resolution committee had refused to offer a much longer resolu tion along the same lines, which Ja cobs hnd presented to them in the morning, in their report to the con vention. At the morning session Jacobs had practically been hooted down by a cer tain number of delegates when he read his original resolution. As a result the resolution committee embodied an emas culntod form of the resolution, as one of them admitted on the floor, "with the sting taken out." It was a harmless group of words, "heartily Indorsing the president ot the United States and the interstate com merce commission in working toward stopping rebate discrimination," and end ing with an abruptness which wns ap parently painful to Jacobs, because hla amendment was to be tacked to tho sen tence in such a way that it stood out with a strength that put the preceding clfiuse Into a useless Introduction. There was a strenuous objection to tlie nmendment, on the ground that the com mittee on resolutions preferred to have everything prepared in brief form, and thought Jacobs' amendment too long, so hud left it out. Jacobs jumped to his feet. "Do you mean to tell these delegates that you are afraid to have this state enforce the laws? For twelve years our railroad commission has been sound asleep, except when they woke up to draw their salaries. It is time we. woke up ourselves and took some action to preserve our industries and our rights. Afraid to Enforce Laws "Are there some people in the state getting special privileges, so that they are afraid to ask that the laws be en forced? Are you going to put yourselves on record us wanting equal laws for all, or are you going to take a stand for emasculated laws and deliver yourselves of a lot ot platitudes? 'Let us do something. During the com ing year the dominant subject before the people of this state will be the railroads. We want a -square deal from the rall roais and this amendment only asks that the state of California do for us what the national government Is doing for the whole country, and that is— simply en force tho laws." Secretary Rufus P. Jennings asked that the amendment be read again, and then Dr. I*. A. Perce of Los Angeles exlpained why the resolution committee had not adopted the amendment. "It was all threshed out," he said, "but hasty action on such things Is not good. None of Mr. Jacobs' statements Is un true, but as business men this is the proposition: When his statement is in the resolution why do we need a repetition of words to make it stronger, when the only strength they could add would be condemnatory, statements on certain lines. We should not call forth a storm of protest from those who are serving us. "Personally I am not interested. I pay my own railroad fare and am under no obligations to the common carriers, yet at the same time it is not necessary to decry the interests of the common car-; riers to get those things we should have and will have." Tarpey had the floor, and before he had had his say those oppoued to attacking "common car riers" saw the strategy of Jacobs unfold itself, for Mr. Tarpey launched the full resolution, which after a stormy scene was adopted. The resolution is as follows: "Whereas, It Is recognized that truns portatlon companies are the leading fac tors in the development of new trade for the marketing and distribution of our products; and, "Whereat. It is necessary in order that our products .should gain as wide a dis tribution as possible that transportation companies should strictly comply with the lawe and afford every necessary facil ity without discrimination or favor to any individual v corporation; and, "Whereas. The developments recently, as indicated by the testimony introduced before the Interstate commissioner. Hon. Franklin K. Lane, at San Francisco, dem onstrates the most amazing and flagrant disregard for the law _y Individuals, cor porations end transportation companies; and, '"Whereas, California is the only Pacific coast state that Is not enforcing the laws and regulations governing transportation companies; and, "Whereas, Legislation is absolutely nec Los Angeles Herald. essary to remedy and eradicate the bur densome conditions, evils and discrimina tions from which California shippers, pro ducers and manufacturers are now suf fering; and, "Whereas, The domination of legisla tive bodies and the strangling of neces sary legislative enactment Is owing to the Interference In politics of active authorized secret agents of the trans portation companies; therefore, be it Keep Out of Politics "Resolved, That In the interests of Cali fornia industries we demand that all transportation companies, either through their avowed 'or secret agents, or other wise, do refrain from action in our politi cal affairs, and do attend to their legiti mate business as common carriers under the law, doing which we pledge them our support and assistance In their every legitimate endeavor. "Resolved, by the counties committee of California, That we do hereby denounce the violations and evasions of laws gov erning transportation companies as being Inimical to California's best Interests and tending to debauch our body politic. "Resolved, That we hereby place our selves on record for equal rights to all and special privileges to none in rates and handling of transportation. "Resolved, That we stand for and advo cate the strict enforcement of the laws governing and regulating transportation companies and will encourage by every means in our power such new legislation as will be necessary to regulate and im prove the service regarding car shortages, demurrages and all unjust exactions and discriminations. MINNEAPOLIS, Dec. 14.— Sitting in the automobile and carried for fifty yards on the cow-catcher of a passenger engine, every Instant expecting to be ground be neath the wheels of the train, was the harrowing experience of S. J. Hewson, president of the Menomlnee Hydraulic Pressed Brick company, and Frank Peck, superintendent of the Menomlnee branch of the company in Minneapolis, last night. They escaped, however, without a bruise. Declaring It H->rs, Loses Ap peal to Superior Court In the suit of Ltda Colburn against Anita Shaffer for the recovery of a pony which the defendant claimed as her prop erty, Judge Monroe decided In favor of the plaintiff yesterday, the defendant not appearing in court. The case was ap pealed from Justice Stephens' court early in July, where it had been decided in favor of the plaintiff. The testimony brought out the most startling horse stories on record, the wit nesses for the defense claiming that their horse had not died, but had been dyed and even rejuvenated, for the horse they claimed was only twelve years younger than the date of his birth seemed to Bhow In December, 1905, Miss Shaffer sent a bay pony to the pasture of Wing brothers at Alhambra. A few weeks later the pony died and the owner was notified by mail. She claimed to have been out of the state when the letter was sent, and when she returned last spring she saw a pony resembling hers, except for the color, in charge of a small boy. Without any further explanation she took possession of the horse and the suit for recovery followed. In the J trial Miss Shaffer insisted that the pony she had seized was the one she had sent to the Wing pasture and that instead of having died there it had been stolen and subsequently dyed. In support she offered the testimony of a pharmacist who had formerly been a horse doctor, and he claimed the hair on the pony was stiff and showed other evidence of having been dyed. He said also the pony was at least 16 years old. Mrs. Colburn, on the other hand, in sisted the pony was a 4-year-old and had been in her possession more than two years. She ridiculed the dye theoryJustice Stephens said: "There seems to be considerable conflict of evidence In this case, but the fact that the pony died in the pasture seems well established." Judge Monroe yesterday ordered Judg ment for the plaintiff or damages in the sum of $100 in case the horse could not be recovered, with $25 costs. WASHINGTON, Dec. 18.— "The en gineers of the Panama canal commission are perfectly willing that the Socks should be widened to any extent the navy thinks necessary. Goethals, chairman of the commission. Col. MOORE'S ATTITUDE IS SUSTAINED JOS. SCOTT TELLS TEACHERS HIS INTERPRETATION HE HAS DELVED DEEPLY INTO SCHOOL LAW Frank F. Bunker Makes Excellent Speech on Conception of Educa tion and Its Real Object. Pedagogues Show Interest Yesterday the sessions of the Los An geles city and county teachers in the an nual Teachers' institute were augmented by the opening of tho Southern California Teachers' association with Its fifteenth annual session last night. The program throughout the day was one calculated to bring much good to the children under the charge of the tpHchers who participated In the events. One of the principal events of the ses sion was the speech of Joseph Scott, president of the board of education, who made a stirring address, straight to the point, indorsing the position taken by Dr. Moore, the superintendent, on religious training in the school. Mr. Scott Is well known for his etraightforward speeches, and yesterday was no exception. He said: "Assigned to me for this morning's program is the topic of 'Moral Bduca tlon,' the subject having been allotted to me about two weeks ago. I have just -returned from a week's absence to the northern part of the state, and on my return I am confronted with a situ ation In our department which cannot be Ignored by me unaer the topic of my nddr'ese. Since my return I have been in receipt of a letter from a most es timable gentleman in this city, a per sonal friend of mine, expressing the hope that I. as a 'good Catholic' would see that the name of Christ was given due consideration in the Christmas exercises. I was not aware that I was serving on the board of education as a good Catholio or in any other capacity than as a good citizen, and this is the first time any reference has been made to the character of my religion during my three years' career as a member of the board of ed ucation. Demanded by Statutes "I have been compelled on previous occasions to give some attention to the constitutionality of the law of the state of California in reference to this matter of sectarian or denominational education, and I am compelled to the belief that we have no right under the law to at tempt any doctrinal or dogmatic teach ings as to the divinity of Christ. Four of my children attend the public schools, and It is needless to say it would be an uplift to them and to their parents if the beautiful story of Christmas, -.vith all Its pathos and piety, could be Introduced Into the Christmas exercises; but having a conscientious belief that my oath of of fice debars me from consenting to any thing of that kind, I need only say that I concur in the opinion of Dr. Moore, as he has given It to me In reference to his order issued to the principals of the different schools. I do not know his exact phraseology; probably he does not recall it himself. Certainly no one who has taken it at hearsay can be ex pected to reproduce it exactly; but he advises me that the order Is similar in character to what has been issued on previous occasions, namely, prohibiting any doctrinal or dogmatic reference to Christ. "That 98 per cent of our children, ac cording to the judgment of learned di vines, believe in the divinity of Christ does not justify me In thwarting the law. Might was never right 'In foro consclentlae'; and while we Christian people are in the overwhelming majority In this community and every other, we must stillsupport the rights of the Jew and the agnostic. A member of this board, H. W. Frank, is a member of the Hebrew religion. He has rendered moet excellent service as a member of this board and has been a stalwart and loyal citizen of Los Angeles for years, and the constitution guarantees him the right that the religious opinions of his children shall not be affected by any ex ercises in the public schools., All States Alike "I am not here passing judgment on the law itself. That is a different mat ter. Suffice it to say that every state in the Union has more or less drastic constitutional provisions of a similar character. I do not think I can be charged with having any religious af filiations with the Hebrew race, because I presume my profession of faith Is more or less known to all of you and Is dia metrically opposed to our Hebrew fellow citizens, so I am compelled to suggest to our Christian brethren, clerical and lay, that they deal with the question at Sac ramento and before the voters of the state and not submit to the members of the department of this board of education the temptation to violate their oath of office for the purpose of obtaining favor in the sight of a certain portion of the Christian people. Remember that the lowest creature that walks 1« the cow ard, and the lowest of all cowards is the iwnrd. A man can simply do his duty and then face the consequence* without fliuoiilng, and I believe Dr. Moore LOS ANGELES HERALD: THURSDAY MORNING, DECEMBER 19, 1907. to have been so actuated and to have so done." Frank F. Bunker, assistant superintend ent of city schools, spoke on the relation ship of the teachers as Individuals In the school work. He said in part: "In casting about for a theme of suffi cient worth and dignity to bear 'presenting to you teachers, one thought has kept continually forcing itself before my at tention—a thought which Indeed for years has been gradually clearing Itself from out the chaos whence emerge all our thoughts — a thought which has bone far toward making clear to me, In a rela tive degree at least, many of the perplex-, itles and mysteries which life holds In store for every one of her children. It is the thought that the eoul of one has pos sibilities for growth, and that life, this life, rich, abundant, complex, when seen In proper perspective and in its true sig nificance, is but a eeries of opportunities making for soul growth. Discusses Education "In the light of this thought permit me to discuss briefly the significance of the great work of education in which we are all engaged and our Individual relation ship to our work. "When viewed in the large education Is seen to be a vastly greater process than that comprehended in our institution of the school, and yet, by reason of the prominence of the school through the splendid support accorded it t>y the etate and nation, and by reason of our own close proximity to our own work as teachers, rrsiny of us have cause to feel that the school is the chief, and Indeed the solo instrument of education. The many phrases one hears in common par lance — 'My son will complete his educa tion at so and so's institution this year.' 'Poor fellow, he had to drop out of col lege before completing his education," or 'Yes, she's a good woman, but her edu cation Is somewhat lacking,'— all these phrases and many more betoken the same conception on the part ct the general pub lic; the conception that education can be measured in terms of quantity of school ing. "To this notion some of our university presidents have contributed, to a degree at least, for In some Instances there are those who have declared that no one Khali ever be eligible to appointment on their faculties who does not possess a doctor's degree, which shows that the holder has spent a definite and required number of years in the technical work of the school. False Conception "The tendency, too, in many quarters to hold the schools responsible for the class of educated criminals which infests our cities grows out likewise from the same false conception. "The fact that Abraham Ruef passed through all the grades of our public schools and graduated from the state uni versity with honor while Francis J. Heney waa expelled from the same In stitution on grounds of general cussed ness, has given point to many a criticism upon the work of the schools. Yet long before there were schools, in the sense of which we ordinarily use the term, there were educated people, men and wo men of splendid ideals of character and conduct. There are today in the ac qualnanceship of each one of you many men and women educated in the larger sense and possessing fine ideals who have had little or no work In the public schools. "In an absolute sense It is utterly im possible over to wholly neglect education. We are being educated in spite of our selves, for the world Is penetrating through our senses, and deep down in the human soul there is a reaction contin ually in progress— a reaction set up by the universe. "In a very real sense, as someone has said, 'The old world is the great school master,' and men and women and boys and girls are being educated by it, ctase lessly and inevitably. I would be the last one in the world to belittle the work of our schools, for I have an abiding faith and confidence in them; neither would I lessen one whit the responsibility for the shaping of character and conduct which should in proper degree be placed on the shoulders of tho men and women who are connected with the institution of the school, yet I contend that any discussion of the significance of the function of the school fall 3 very far wide of the mark which fails to recognize that the school process is a part of a very much larger world process by which society is work ing out Its destiny. "This society of which I speak, and by which I mean humanity in the ag gregate, may bo likened to a great or ganism—living, breathing, moving, chang ing. Men are born into It, they live their lives; they exert an influence, little or great; they pass out of it; others take their places and still society keeps on living and breathing and moving and changing. "Thus it has ever been down through all the ages; thus it will ever be till the end of time. Climbing up to some van tage point whence one can look out and down upon this great organism and one sees much to perplex and confuse. There is much of a running to and fro; there is much of tumult and confusion; there la much of a strange shouting. When ona asks the reason why, no reason is given. Rugby Football "The spectator on the bleachers at a game of. Rugby football one moment sees a whirling, swirling tangle of arms and legs; the next moment the aggregation rushes oft In a given, direction as though Impelled by one mind, then they rush back; then they all go over to the side lines and Ho down; then they get up, come back to the starting place and the strange performance Is repeated. It would be a bold fellow who, seated on the bleachers and before the game had closed, sought to plat the path by which the goal is reached. Just so wit'the observer of the perplexing and CQ movements of the members and'parta of this social organism of which i speak. It is Indeed a bold prophet who attempts to point the path by which society will reach its goal. NEW YORK, Dec. 20.— William H. Taft, secretary of war, returned today from his trip around the world, bringing renewed assurances of Japan's friendliness toward the United States, but declining to say anything with respect to the political sit uation in this country. He said he had been too long out of Intimate touch with political affairs at home to discuss them In any way. One of Mr. Taft's interviewers had the temerity to ask: "Well, Mr. Secretary, tell us who is your choice for president." Amid general laughter, In which he joined, the secretary replied: "I guess I will have to leave that for inference." Mr. Taft left for Washington on an early afternoon train, saying that accu mulated matters in the war department would keep his nose to the official grind stone for some time to come and that preparation of hts special report on the Philippines, which would be in book form, would also require much of his time in th") near future. Chased by Reporters During his two hours' stay In New York Mr. Taft was aboard the army tug Gen eral Johnston, which had taken him from the liner President Grant at quarantine. Newspaper men who had gone down the bay to meet the returning secretary reached the steamer's side after he had been transferred, and then followed a lively chase In an endeavor to overhaul the army boat with the crested and four starred flag of the secretary of war fly ing at the masthead. The Johnston nad been placed at the disposal of Henry W. Taft, the secre tary's brother, by Gen. F. D. Grant, com manding the department of the east, yho also went down c.i the Johnston to pay his respects. First the secretary was carried to Jer sey City to find out about trains, and there it was announced that he would re ceive the newspapermen at West Twenty third street, New York, at a given hour. The small army of reporters who gath ered at the pier found they were again a few minutes late. Away went the re porters again, and the secretary was inally overhauled Just as was about to take the train for Washington. He was most cordial In manner, and laughingly remarked, that he was sorry to have been "lost" so long in the harbor and that he had caused so much trouble. Looking exceedingly well, the secretary said he had taken daily five-mile walks on the decks of the Grant during the thirteen days' trip from Hamburg. Talk of War Foolish "It is the height of foolishness to talk of possible war with Japan," deplared the secretary. "Japan does not desire war with us, and we certainly do not desire war with Japan. If there was any war spirit anywhere in Japan I failed to nnd the slightest dot of It. Everywhere there was talk of continued peace. "I speak .very confidently about this. Our trade relations with Japan are ex tensive and constantly growing. Japan s exports amount annually to about $160, 00,000, of which we take about one-third. The exports consist largely of mattings, lace goods, embroideries and other fancy work, in the production of which many people are Interested. We, in turn, ship vast quantities of flour, oil and such com modities to Japan. This sort of trade 18 a great pacificator." "What about the Pacific fleet? "The sailing must have been a mag nificent sight. We have fine chips and fine personnel, and as long as the Pa cific ocean belongs to us as much as to anyone else I see no reason why we should not send our ships there on a practice cruise. The Japanese arc too intelligent and high minded to attribute any false motive to the movement. "My trip had as its only definite ob ject a trip to the Philippines. My trip to Japan was only incidental. TravelIng by commercial steamer, we had to stop there, and it was only courtesy for me to pay my respects to the emperor. The trip through Russia was made part ly to save time and partly because I had crossed the Pacific six timfs and was rather anxious to see the territory. My visit was in no sense official. "So many courtesies were shown me from the moment I put foot on Russian soil that I could not have refused even had I desired to do so the Invitation to an audience with the Russian emperor. I was much impressed by the emperor's personality and his entire familiarity with current affairs, especially Ameri can politics. Host Target for Bomb "At Moscow I had the rather novel experience of dining one day with an offioial who next day was. made the target of a bomb, 'mis was Governor General Gurschellman. A ride through Siberia was moat enlightening and gave one a very different ideaof that coun try from what it is generally conceived to be. Especially Is this true as to agri culture, minerals and 'population. "Western Siberia will probably under go the same process of development ac our middle west. I believe that in time it will be the center of population of the Russian empire. "I was much pleased with condltlors In the Philippines. They were much better than I had hoped for. The Initial proceedings of the first Philippine as sembly and its tendency toward conserv atism despite the supposed radical ma jority was most gratifying.
