Bertha Vaughn Renders "Chan son Provencal d?l Aqua" Before Southern California Teach ers' Association "The chief word in the old training was 'don't.' The chief word In the new training 1b 'do,' " said Superintendent James L. Hughes of Toronto before the Southern California Teachers' associa tion yesterday afternoon at its session in Temple auditorium. Superintendent A. J. Adrian, president of the association, Introduced Mme. Ber tha Vaughn, who rendered "Chanson Provencal del Augua." Superintendent Hughes was the first speakc.-. His topic was "The Old Train ing end the New." He said In part: "Every child has three great central tendencies as soon as It Is able to walk. It loves to do things, to do things It plans itself and to do things In co-operation with otherd. These are the greatest elements in human character; they are the elements that have enabled mankind to achieve a progressive civilization. These three tendencies should be the dominant ele ments in the life of every man at ma turity. The old training robbed every man of these tendencies. The more thoroughly a boy was trained under the old Ideal the less Initiative and force and originality and transforming power and achieving tendency he had. There Is little use in preaching from the text •B^e ye doers of the word and not nearers only" so long as men and women are trained to be don'ters. The word training is used three times in the Bible, and the derivative meaning of the word in each case Is to clear away difficulties. The old training has degraded training so as to make It mean some form of adult interference. Old Ider 1 Negative "The Ideal of self control under the old training was the power of keeping away from wrong. This is merely a negative ideal. The old training dealt with nega tive characteristics, the new training deals with tne positive elements of char acter. The old training was engaged most of the time in stopping the child's doing, the new training aims continuous ly to develop tne child's tendency to do. Achieving tendency and power are the ends most desired by the new training. A man may possess the self control that keeps him away from every form of evil, and yet be of no more service to God and his fellowmen than a grass hopper. True self control, positive self control, the self control of the new train ing, means the control that each man should have over his physical, intellec tual and spiritual powers to enable him to achieve his best work for humanity and God. "The old training regarded self-con sciousness as a weakness in character. .There are two kinds of self-conscious /ness—the one of weakness and the other of strength. The old training made the child conscious of weakness, the new training makes him conscious of his highest power. Responsibility for Good "The old Ideal of responsibility was •Jiegative; the new ideal Is positive. The old training taught our responsibility for the wrong that we do; the new training -teaches our responsibility for the achieve ment of the good we have special power to do. There Is no vitality in a sense of responsibility for the wrong that we do. A consciousness of Individual power and of responsibility for its use Is the Strongest propelling moral element in character. "The old ideal of law was negative; the new ideal is positive. The old train ing made law restrictive, the new train ing makes law directive. All children naturally reverence law and they would continue to reverence It if it was ad ministered directively and not restrlctive ly. The child formerly found law to be in opposition to the achievement of his plans, whereas under true training law is the child's guiding friend, enabling him to produce greater results by his efforts. Law aids the child to greater achievement under the new training; un der the old training its chief function was to restrict his efforts. The supreme aim of the trainer of a child in 'regard to law should be to develop his natural, reverence for the laws of a game into a related progressive sequence of rev erence for law In the home, for lnw In the school, for law in the state and be yond this to a reverence for the laws of his ow»t life and for the laws of God. The new training tries to develop rever ence for law and not mere submission to any individual Elders Tyrannical "The old ideal of obedience was nega tive; the new ideal Is positive. The old training, when it demanded obedience really meant conscious subordination. Children are naturally obedient and they would continue to be co-operatively dbe dlent if parents and teachers were not tyrannical. If men ordered each other to do things in the same tone and man ner used by adults in ordering children to do things, 'what a sensation would be caused! "The old training In courtesy was neg ative, the new training alms to be posi tive. The old training said, 'Children should be seen and not heard,' and 'Chil dren should speak when they are spoken to.' It is surely as unmannerly for a father to Interrupt his child when he is speaking as for the chUd to interrupt his father. It is strange that adulthood, should claim a monopoly of the right to be discourteous. Courtesy begets cour tesy. 'The old criticism mada the ohUd con scious of failure; the new criticism makes the child conscious of his success. "The motive of the old training was tho negative motive— fear; the motive of the new training Is the positive motive oC genuine sympathy. God Use i as Threat "Even God himself was used negatively by the old training. Audacious adult hood said to the child, "God won't love you if you do that.' or *God will be very angry with you If you do that.' One happy child said when told that God would not love her: 'Oh, well, Moses will!' A little boy, when his mother said, 'God will be very angry.' replied. Foreign Minister Viscount Hayashi sent his regrets, his absence be ing due to an official entertainment In honor of the Korean crown prince. Viscount Kaneko, on toasting Ambassa dor O'Brien, eald that the society was organized for the purpose of having It become an Intellectual bridge connecting the Pacific coasts of two nations who had assumed the joint responsibility of main taining peace on the Pacific, therefore the greater the naval power of America the less would be the burden of Japan. Moore, Wisconsin Volunteers, Happy by Noble Act [Special to The Herald.] ROCK ISLAND, II!., Oct. 16.—After having been lost forty-three years, the love letters which Mrs. Frank Young wrote to her soldier-sweetheart during the Civil war were returned to her to duy through the agency of J. H. McCutcheon, an ex-Confederate soldier living in Los Angeles. Incidentally the return of the missing epistles ends a search for the rightful owner begun when the war closed and continued with more or less vigor ever since. The story behind the return of the letters is tilled with romance and proves that although Blue and Gray fought each other with all the passion of belief In a cause, there were some among the fighters who had the nobility of true manhood within their breasts. When the bloody battle of Gettys burg was being fought and when the Union troops were being mowed down like wheat in the harvest, the Con federates charged upon Gettysburg station, a position held by the enemy. During the charge Private McCutcheon stumbled upon an inert and apparently lifeless body, beside which lay a port folio. That was the first day of the battle of Gettysburg, July 1. 1563. McCutcheon was attached to Com pany H of the Fifth Virginia infantry, one of the divisions kept constantly on the move during the battle of Gettys burg and for many days after. Fol lowing the battle McCutcheons com pany was sent hurriedly to a position far removed from where he had found the wallet, and it had almost become forgotten in the stress of the times. McCutcheon made Investigation of the wallet's contents and discovered It to contain numerous letters, most of them love letters, signed Bertha. The letters were addressed to "Dear Ed," but the envelopes were missing. After learning the character of the letters McCutcheon vowed that he would some day return them to tlje writer, and as soon as the war closed began his search. It so happened that Private E. E. [By Associated Press.] BAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 21.—The great parade of civic and industrial organizations held here today wa-i marred by what might have been a fatal accident when the spirited horse ridden by Nicholas Covarrublas, im personating Don Gaspar de Portola, fell backward with his rider. With incomparable horsemanship Don Gaspar rolled from under his falling steed, and the great throng, which had grown as still as death In expecation of a tragedy about to bJ enacted before it, broke forth in wave after wave of heartfelt cheers. Colonel yon Schroeder, who was rid ing at the head of the Fourteenth United States cavalry, which formed the military escort of Don Gaspar de Portola and Queen Virgilia, assisted the gallant Spaniard to his feet. Although badly shaken and bruised by his fall, he insisted upon remount ing his horse, and on finding that the bridle was ruined beyond repair, he fastened two handkerchiefs around the horse's neck and rejoined the queen at the head of the procession. Before the accident Don Gaspar had reined his horse in so that he could salute the cheering crowds with both hands. While thus held In check, the spirited animal reared and went over so suddenly that the horror-stricken spectators' scarcely realized his dan ger before the gritty don was on hia feet. SAYS INCARCERATION DUE TO CONSPIRACY DOCTOR IN INSANE ASYLUM MAKES GRAVE CHARGES Grand Jury in Honolulu Declares the Accusations Made by Physician Unworthy of Consideration by Its Body HONOLULU, Oct. 21.—United States Circuit Judge de Bolt has given the federal grand jury a special charge concerning the case of Dr. John Atch erly, who Is conlined in the asylum for the insane. Dr. Atcherly, who claims to have dis covered a cure for leprosy, and has a large native following, charges that his incarceration is the result of a con spiracy inspired by the jealousy of local physicians. The matter was called to the atten tion of the members of congress who visited the islands recently, but they declined to take action. Judge de Bolt' calls the grand jury's attention to the allegation that Dr. Atcherly Is confined in the asylem ow ing to an alleged unlawful conspiracy entered into by Territorial Secretary E. A. Mott-Smith, Attorney General Hemenway, City and County Attorney Cathcart, District Magistrate Andrade, Sheriff Jarrett, Circuit Judge Lindsay and several leading physicians. Under the circumstances, Judge de Bolt says, the attorney general and his deputies are disqualified from handling the case. He suggests that the jury conduct Its own investigation without the aid of government counsel. On the request of Judge de Bolt the grand Jury Immediately convened, and after a short session declared the charges of conspiracy made against a number of federal and territorial offi cials by Dr. Atcherly were unworthy of serious consideration. OPPOSES SHIP SUBSIDY BILL SENATOR NEWLANDS GIVES HIS REASON FOR OPPOSITION Nevada Solon Says Country Cannot Compete with Other Nations in Carrying Trade Under Pro. tective Tariff RENO, Ne'v., Oct. 26.—Senator ; Francis G. Newlands made public toI night his answer to James McNab, I president of the San Francisco cham ber of commerce, who had written ask ing the senator's view regarding the passage by congress of a ship subsidy law. Mr. Newlands said he opposed the subsidy and advocated rather the United States build an auxiliary fleet to be leased to private persons in time of peace. The senator said that under the protective tariff the United States could ,not hope to compete with other nations in the carrying trade. The letter follows: "My dear sir: I am in receipt of your letter of September 13 in which you call my attention to the 'blight that has fallen on Pacific coast ship ping Interests' and state that 'in the last analysis, unless American ship ping interests on the Pacific be prop erly promoted and protected, the great manufacturing and producing Interests In the interior of the country, and the labor interwoven therein, will feel most keenly the extinction of American ship ping in Pacific waters.' "I have also read, with great in terest, your letters to the editor of the American Flag, the Hon. George C. Perkins, and to the secretary of the navy, all of them showing that it Is impossible for American vessels, manned with American crews, to com pete in the International transporta tion with foreign ships because of the higher cost—both of construction and operation—of American ships, and the necessity therefore of liberal subsidies by the national government in order to rehabilitate the American merchant marine. Vessels Cost More to Build Here "Your letter to the secretary of the navy makes comparison of the Ameri ican vessel Wilhelmina with a foreign ship, showing that the Wilhelmlnn, constructed in America, cost double what it would have cost if constructed in England, and showing that this ves sel, without counting the difference in cost of feeding the crew and other items, must cam $12,750 more than a foreign vessel on a voyage of sixty days' or in other words, that if the foreign vessel should receive $3.35 per ton the American vessel should re ceive $6.53 per ton for carrying coal for the navy, Illustrates the hopeless character of attempting to rebuild our marine engaged in foreign trade save by a colossal subsidy, which the peo ple would not tolerate. "You urge, in view of these facts, that the 50 per cent extra offered by the navy department to Ajnerican ships for the transportation of coal over what foreign vessels would charge is not sufficient and that this should be in creased to X P°r cent. "The same reasoning would require the encouragement of the American merchant marine by subsidy which would enable the American ships to receive for transportation in the freight charge nnd in the subsidy received double the amount charged by foreign ships for a -similar service. The enor mous burden which would thus be im posed upon the taxpayers of the coun try can hardly be measured. Cost Must Be Lessened "This is the initial step to take, and the establishment of a merchant ma rine will accomplish nothing until the tost of production in our country is diminished. "If anything is to be done in this direction I would favor the immediate construction of ships as part of an auxiliary system of the American navy, letting them out In times of peace to private corporations and establishing on them a naval reserve, so that both the ships and men could be made use of in case of war, In preference to any system of subsidizing private ship companies. We have gone far enough in Kianting special privileges and in subsidizing special interests and we should retreat from the position al ready assumed rather than advance further In this direction. "Very sincerely yours, "FRANCIS G. NEWLANDS." Rose McMahon was friendly with the Yon Royens. This caused MoMahon to dislike her. Fearing mob violence by a throng gathered about the county Jail after the confession, the authorities tonight rushed the murderer and his brother, Patrick McMahon, and Patrick Lamb, a farm hand, who are held as witnesses in the case, to the Kansas state peni tentiary at Lansing. McMahon took sole responsiDUlty and especially exonerated his brother, as he feared the officers would charge him with complicity. McMahon told a friend today where he had hidden the revolver with which he did the killing and several articles he took out of the Van Royen home. The sheriff went to the designated place and found the articles and then decided to arrest J .mes McMahon. As he was prepar ing to go aftfr the man, McMahon walked into his office and announced that he was ready to help work on the case, as he has been doing each day since the tragedy. Immediately Arrested Becker immediately arrested him, and without telling of the evidence he took McMahon to his home, where he also arrested Patrick McMahon and Lamb. "Yes, I killed my two sisters and borther-in-law, and I was crazy when I did it," he shouted, rising out of his chair and pacing the room. "It took me three months to plan and execute the crime. I dragged his body across the creek and then prepared to finish the deed. Plans Murder of Sisters "For an hour I wandered about, planning. Then I walked into the house. "My first shot probably killed Mrs. Van Royen as she sat on a chair. She screamed and fell. Rose started up to speak to me, and I shot her dead. MUSHET AND THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS—IV Showing How the Enemies of the Public Schools Inter fered with the Sale of the School Bonds pBinHEN the people, disregarding the attacks on the school bond issue made by WWt Mr. Mushet and his accomplice in his fight against the public schools of the I\™ I I city, the Los Angeles Times, carried this bond issue by a vote of more than Bklb/Bi 3 to 1, the good citizens believed that the fight for adequate school facilities /or the childreri of the city of Los Angeles was ended and that never again would buys and girls of the city in search of an education have to encamp for twenty-four hours upon the steps, of its school buildings in order to be registered as scholars. After the bonds were voted preparations were made for issing them and the officials charged with their sale ascertained that although bearing only 4% interest they could be sold for something of a premium, so eager was the investing public at this particular lime, just after the panic, to put its money in securities that were regarded as abso lutely sound. Rut when the bonds were about to be sold the good people of the city, and especially the parents of children who were depending upon the public schools for an education, were astounded by the bringing of an action in the name of one Spencer to set aside the bond issue and declare the bonds void on account of certain alleged irregulari ties in the election. Mr. Spencer was a small property owner in the city of Los Angeles but not by any means wealthy enough to have assumed the burden of such a litigation. An investiga tion has shown that Mr. Spencer was backed by five individuals who each agreed to contribute a share to the expense of bringing and maintaining the suit. Just who these individuals were and whether or not Mr. Mushet, the city auditor, was one of them, The Herald is unable to state, although it is able to state most positively that there were five men who pledged themselves to defray the expenses of the litigatisn. The Herald can, and does, state positively that before Mr. Spencer brought his suit and while he was preparing for it he had one or more interviews with Mr. Mushet, and The Herald has no, doubt, and it believes no intelligent citizen of the city has any doubt, that in these inter views Mr. Mushet not only consented to but encouraged the bringing of this action. It is fairly certain also that had it not been for the encouragement given by Mr. Mushet by his various attacks upon the administration of the public schools, the opponents of the schools would not have had the courage to bring this suit. The Los Angeles Times has been severely criticised by citizens for its share in the at tacks upon the public schools. It should be remembered, however, that its attacks were founded upon statements made by Mr. Mushet, and if the Times is to be criticised for using, as a public journal, the utterances of a public official of the city derogatory to the administration of city affairs by another department of the city government, then how much more does the man making these utterances—-utterances which were found by two investigating committees to be false and unfounded—deserve the criticism of the public. So that whether or not Mr. Mushet contributed any financial assistance to the action brought against the school bonds and which tied up their sale for months, it is very evident that the encouragement which he had in the past given the opponents of the school bonds was largely responsible for the action of Mr. Spencer which prevented the sale of the school bonds for months, so that needed improvements in the public schools could not be made, and as a result many boys and girls were compelled to camp at the begin ning of the last term not for twenty-four hours bat for forty-eight hours, before the school buildings in order to secure an opportunity for an education. It is, and should be, the pride of the city of Los Angeles that our schools are free and open to the poorest child in our city. When tht school session began hundreds of children who were seeking an education were compelled to seek it in the most uncomfortable and unsanitary condi tions, all as a result of the fight against the public schools of the city of Los Angeles which for more than a year had been led by Mr. Mushet. Iva D. Baladen. It year old son of fiomer A. Baladen was found dead Saturday morning, November *. The body iwas placed on a small terrace in the bank along the public road, about one block from the boy's home, and the same distance from the Butler county court house. In the center of the boy's forehead was a bullet wound, while on his body lay a 41-callber Colt revolver, the property of his father. Non-committal In the verdict was rendered this morning, the Jury, which has been sitting In the case at various times during the last week, has admit ted Its Inability to cope with the situa tion. It has left open to the parents and friends of ths dead boy an oppor tunity to prosecute a vigorous search for the author of. the crime. The verdict reads as follows: "We, the members of the Jury find that the said Iva D. Baisden came to his death by a pistol or rifle ball at the hands qf an unknown party." Sensation is Hinted. That a woman, prominently connect ed In Greenville, Is involved In the case is the opinion of many who have studied its various phasea That a sensational expose will be made in the near future is not an impossibility. Several tacts give color to the theory that a feminine hand may be traced in the crline. The boy's camp of the At*l Friday night was pitched deep ib a thicket in Hawkins' Creek swamp. The location of the camp is accessible with difficulty in daylight. Those who knew young Baisden de olare that he Was unfamiliar with the place and that he either was lured to the spot or was lost in the pitchy night of the woods. There is also evidence to believe that a second person was with Baisden when ho met death, either having followed him. or having laid In ambush for him. The finding of a woman's night robe in the fork of a tree at the boy's camp has thus far been unexplained. Bals den's father has Identified the gown as one which was purchased in Mont gomery last January. a quilt was also taken by the boy. There were other appearances of the camp which would seem to Indicate the presence of a woman. When the body of Baisden was found, three' miles distant from the camp. It had been placed on the quilt, the limbs being carefully arranged and the gun placed In position on the trunk. Some say that a cold-blooded mur derer, if he had brought the body from the woods In which the crime apparent ly was committed. would have taken no pains in disposing of the body. They believe the corpse was placed where it was found by some one who cherished the dead boy in life. It Is also believed that, if a woman is found in connection with the case, she will be of mature years, and one old enough to keep her own counsel. However, those advocating this theory do not believe that the fatal shot was fired by a woman. Prominent names are eblng mentioned In connection with a line or circumstantial evidence. On the part of some of the officials of Butler County there exists an appar ent apathy and Indifference to the case which has caused much chagrin to many Greenville people. ARCONA, second class protected cruiser* of the Ocr • man navy, steamed majesti cally and without effort into Los An geles harbor yesterday afternoon, shortly after 3 o'clock, and Is now moored at the) foot of Fifth street, San Pedro, where she will remain for five days. Immediately after the cruiser made fast committees from the GermanAmerican Alliance and the chamber of commerce. Mayor Alexander and Lieutenant Reinburg of the revenue service welcomed the vessel nnd her officers to the hospitality of Southern California. An immense throng gathered to watch the cruiser steam up the har bor. In the crowd which lined the wharf there were many citizens of Los Angeles and the greater portion of the population of San Pedro and Wilming ton. It was a sight seldom before seen and one which wlill be long re membered, for It is conclusive proof that the harbor Is qualified in every way to be a haven of vessels flying every flag and of every size. The com ing of the Arcona Is another evidence of the growing Importance of l'ort San Pedro and will bring the attention of the world to Los Angeles in a marked manner. It is the first time that a deep draft vessel has sailed Into the inner harbor. The trip was done easily and with no fear by the skipper of the cruiser, for he knew from the sound ings that It was safe for him to anchor anywhere In the inner, habor.'. Entertainment for Crew During the sojourn of the Arcona life will be one round of pleasure and sightseeing for officers and men of the cruiser. Auto rides about the city and to the neighboring points of inter est, luncheons, dinners, dances and banquets, formal and informal, , are on the program. Some of the entertain ment will be undertaken by the Ger man-American alliance, and the other portion of the formal entertainment will be in charge of the chamber of commerce. The ship is of the protected cruiser class* and is designated as a second class vessel. She was commis sioned in 1901 and Is stationed In China. She carries ten rapid fire four inch guns and several Maxims. She is 320 feet long, 26 feet beam and has a 19-foot draught. The present cruise began last September and will be con cluded In January. From Los Angeles the Arcona will go to San Diego for a brief stay and will then sail to Hon olulu. Yokohama and to its home moorings in China. Nov. 21.—The treatment of American meats by Germany and the probability of modification In forth coming negotiations for a trade ar rangement between the two countries is much discussed in German news papers. The bulletin of the Commercial Treaty association, which is opposed to the high protective policy of the govern ment expresses the opinion that some restrictions placed upon American meats are unnecessary from the purely sanitary standpoint and might well be modified in exchange for certain ad vantages under the American tariff law. The association, however, rejects the claim that American animals and meats are subject to exceptional treatment at the 1 Kinds of the German govern ment. The prohibition against the Importa tion of American beef cattle was Issued in 1895 because several animals in two cargoes shipped to Hamburg were dis covered to be affected with Texas fever; but the importation of live cattle from Australia, Russia, Rou niania, Italy and some other countries is also prohibited, but for other rea sons. It Is remarked furthermore that, even If the prohibition of imports from the United States were abrogated, It would still be impossible to bring American cattle into Germany, be cause they, in common with cattle from other over-sea countries, would be subject tp a quarantine detention and observation of four weeks and would have to be put through the tuberculin test. Think It Over, Fellow Villagers HEALY AND HOUGHTON'S SHARE IN RIVERBED FRANCHISE STEAL? SOME of the city councilmen who were concerned in the shameful riverbed franchise steal, the true inwardness of which was explained by Mr. Lelande's affidavit published in yesterday's Herald, were either retired to private life by their constituents, or had enough s«nse of decency left to keep out of the public eye after the expiration of the term of office in which they had so outrageously betrayed the interests of the people intrusted to them. Two men who voted for that infamous measure are yet in the public eye; one a man who notwithstanding that and many other acts of betrayal of the public of which he has constantly been guilty, has been returned to the city council by the Eighth ward of the city, which has for years been content to be represented in that body by councilmen such as Barney Healy and Thomas Savage. The other member of the council who so outrageously betrayed the city, who has had neither the good sense nor the modesty to keep out of the public eye, is Dr. Houghton, who was promptly retired to private life by his constituents for his share in the riverbed franchise and other matters, but who now seeks re-election to the city council not by a ward of the city, but by the great city of Los Angeles as a whole. Inasmuch as these two men are asking for the votes of the people of Los Angeles, to represent them in the city council the body which makes laws for the city and Hrgely transacts its business and administers its finances, it is appropriate to in quire just what share they had in the riverbed franchise infamy upon which Mr. Lelande says Mr. Parker stated: "Money was being spent," and whether or not they received any part of that money. It would appear to be self evident that public officials do things for only three reasons. . First, because the thing that they do is right and meets the approval of their consciences. Second, because the thing they do is popular and will advance them in the regard of their constituents. Third, because they have some private end to gain, which in most cases means the acceptance of a bribe, either in money or in some other form of value. It is very evident that the six councilmen who voted for the riverbed franchise steal did not so vote because it was right. Matters of right legislation are not surreptitiously railroaded through legislative bodies.. . Laws that are right are not made laws under cover of secrecy, and before the public has an opportunity of judging of them, and approving or objecting to them. The ordinance granting the riverbed franchise to Mr. Gilmore was introduced at the end of a day's session when the council chamber was almost vacant except for the presence of the officials in it. It was passed hurriedly. The attempt was made by false representation to Mr. Lelande, to secure his signature, and efforts were afterwards made to bulldoze him into signing it. When the public began to investigate it, it was attempted to be justified to the public by a lie told by the nominal grantee, to wit: That it was intended for a railroad which at that time had no entrance into the city of Los Angeles. All these things Messrs. Kern and Houghton knew when they voted for the franchise the second time, if not the first time. They did not vote for the franchise because it was politic and would add to their popularity with their constituents. Legis lators do not ndopt by stealth legislation which they expect to increase their popularity with their constituents. Everyone knows that the attempt was made to surreptitiously pass the ordinance granting the franchise, and have it signed before the public would know of it, because the men concerned in it, from its proposers to the councilmen who voted for it, all knew that it would be unpopular with the public. If Messrs. Healy and Houghtcn did not vote for the ordinance granting the franchise either because it was* right, or because it was popular, then did they vote for it because by doing so they served their private and financial interests? Mr. Lelande says Mr. Parker told him that "Money was being spent" about the franchise. Will any sensible, sane man believe that either Mi. Healy or Dr. Houghton voted for a matter which was so infamous that it had to be surreptitiously introduced, and the effort made to pass it through before the public became aware of it—voted for a matter which they well knew would be unpopular with their constituents, and would make them unpopular, and did it without some personal emolument to themselve>? We venture to say that no man in this city with intelligence sufficient to entitle him to remain outside the confines of a home for the feeble minded, will believe any such thing. And yet these two men, with this sort of record, in dealing with a public prop erty worth at least $1,000,000, are asking the people of Los Angeles to elect them members of a city council which will have to do with the greatest expenditures of money that this ctiy has ever made in its history. A council which in the course of its existence will have something to say about the expenditure of probably $25,000,000. Will the people trust these great issues involving $25,000,0t0 or more of the public money, to men who in dealing with city property worth a million dollars, attempted to rob the city of it? The very question furnishes its own answer. IT IS UN THINKABLE, IT IS IMPOSSIBLE, IT IS BEYOND ALL REASONABLE CONCEPTION THAT MEN WITH SUCH A RECORD SHOULD AGAIN BE THE RECIPIENTS OF ANY PUBLIC TRUST OR CONFIDENCE WHATEVER AT THE HANDS OF CONSTITUENTS WHOM THEY HAVE ALREADY BETRAYED. They should not only be defeated, but they should be defeated by such an overwhelming majority as will make them for ever in the history of Los Angeles object lessons of the way in which the honest citizens of our city hold faithless' public ser vants responsible for betraying the interests of the public intrusted to their hands. Here is a device of supreme instrumental value to the piano-player. In this phase it has been widely exploited. And as an adjunct and a vital one to the Pianola, it has attained celeThe Week's Program , N exhibition and four recitals are the (catutcs of Metrostyle Week. In a room at Aeolian Hall will be dis played a collection of Pianola music-rolls bearing the original inlerprctations and autographs of the world's greatest composers and artists. Other interesting details connected with the Metrostyle, such as Royal Decorations for its inventor, etc., will be included. On four successive davs, viz: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, there will be held a scries of recitals, in many ways, the most interesting and notable New York has ever witnessed. The instruments used at these icitals will be the Metrostyle Pianola and the great Aeolian Pipe Organ. Eminent soloists of a standing commensurate with the importance of the occa sion, will be heard. The music to be rendered will consist of the most popular and representative works of great composers. These works will be rendered with the personal interpretations of the composers them selves. Here is the motive of Metrostyle Week the demonstration of what the Metrostyle alone of all means ever devised by manaccomplishes. The audience at ihesc recitals will hear a rendering of Grieg's music, of Morzkowski's music, of Chaminadc's music, as true to the individual conceptions of these composers, as though they themselves were the performers. The Wonder of the Metrostyle v g HE public has grown accustomed to seeing it stated that the Metrostyle is a 1 "guide lo interpretation." That it enables anyone to play the Pianola with genuine musician!' feeling and expression. A part of the public knows that this is accomplished by following with the Metrostyle pointer attached to the Pianola's tempo-lever, a red interpretation line marked cm the music-roll. But few yet understand how the interpretation lines get on the rolls. Or who puis them there. The greatest musicians in the world to-day are marking these interpretation lines on Pianola rolls. The most famous composers, orchestra conductors, concert pianists and educators, are indicating their interpre tations in this way, that all posterity may profit by the fruits of their genius and years of labor. Think of it for the first time in the history of music, it is now possible for the creator of a noble masterpiece to indelibly record his detailed conception of just how (7 should be played. Every other means of indicating musical interpretation is relative and inaccurate. Metrostyle interpretations are completely detailed and absolutely correct. A Metrostyle record is not only a com plete and faithful indication of the composer or artist's interpretation. It has a far greater value it is a record of his best interpreta tion and is signed by him as such. Time is required to grasp the full significance of this. Its portent, not only to the player of a Pianola, but to all students of musical production by hand and otherwise is overwhelming. brity throughout the world. In its broader aspect however its services to the very art of music itself the Metrostyle has yet to receive deserved recognition from the public as a. whole. It is by way of accomplishing this of presenting concrete, tangible evidence of the unique office performed by this revolutionary invention that Metrostyle Week has been inaugurated.
